definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, the ancestors (pitaraḥ) depend on the rites of rice-ball and water offerings; when varṇa-mixture follows the destruction of a family, these rites lapse and the ancestors fall (1.42).

name: From mastered senses to serenity and peace (BhG 2.64–66)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Moving among objects with senses free of passion and aversion and under the self's control, the disciplined one attains serenity (prasāda); in serenity all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.64–65); without discipline there is no understanding and no cultivation (bhāvanā), without cultivation no peace, without peace no happiness (2.66).

name: Delight in the self (ātmarati): the one for whom nothing remains to be done

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The person who delights in the self alone, is satisfied and content in the self, has nothing that must be done, no purpose in doing or not doing, and depends on no being for any purpose (3.17–18). Commentators divide on whether this exempts such a person from action; the next verse (3.19) still enjoins unattached action.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action binds: the world is bound by action except action done for sacrifice (3.9); one yoked with the understanding of yoga casts off this bondage (2.39), leaves behind good and evil deeds (2.50) and, abandoning the fruit, is freed from the bondage of birth (2.51); those who follow the teaching with faith are released from actions (3.31).

relations.note: action done as yoga, without attachment and for sacrifice, does not bind

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What one attains who abides in the brahmic state (brāhmī sthiti) of steady wisdom even at the time of death (2.72).

name: Not unsettling the understanding of the ignorant

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The knower should not create a split in the understanding (buddhibheda) of the ignorant attached to action, but, acting with discipline, lead them to all actions (3.26); the one who knows the whole should not unsettle the slow who do not (3.29).

name: From dwelling on objects to ruin (BhG 2.62–63)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: For one who dwells on sense objects attachment arises; from attachment desire; from desire anger; from anger delusion; from delusion confusion of memory; from loss of memory destruction of understanding; from that one perishes (2.62–63).

notes: The skeleton records the same sequence as the obstacle obs:chain-from-dwelling-on-objects.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa has nothing to do and nothing to gain in the three worlds, yet keeps acting, for if he did not, people would follow his path, the worlds would perish and he would be the maker of confusion (3.22–24).

relations.note: the Lord's own action is given as the example for acting to hold the world together

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna, his nature struck by pitiable weakness and his mind bewildered about dharma, asks what is decisively better, declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple (śiṣya) who has taken refuge (prapanna), and asks to be instructed (2.7); the teaching follows from 2.11. Droṇa's disciple Dhṛṣṭadyumna leads the opposing army (1.3).

name: The guṇas as the doers of action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: No one remains without acting, being made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti (3.5); all actions are done by the guṇas, and the one deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower of the truth about guṇas and actions thinks 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' and is not attached (3.28); those deluded by the guṇas are attached to their workings (3.29); beings follow their own nature (3.33).

name: The eternal, unslayable embodied one (dehin / śarīrin)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The embodied one is eternal, indestructible, immeasurable, unborn, everlasting and primeval; it neither slays nor is slain and is not slain when the body is slain; weapons, fire, water and wind do not affect it; it is all-pervading, stable, unmoving, unmanifest, unthinkable and unchangeable; it passes into another body as through the ages of life and as one changes clothes; hence it is not to be grieved for (2.12–30).

relations.note: The embodied one is unchanged while it passes from body to body.

notes: Merger: probably the same as the skeleton's broader cpt:the-self (BhG 2.11–30 etc.); both extractors used this id, so it is kept; flagged for the de-duplication pass.

name: No embodied being can remain without action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: No one ever remains even for a moment without acting; all are made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti (3.5); even the maintenance of the body needs action (3.8); even the person of knowledge acts according to his nature (3.33).

name: Desire (and anger) as the enemy (BhG 3.36–43)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: What impels a person to sin against his will is desire, and anger, arising from rajas, all-devouring and greatly sinful — the enemy (3.37); it covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, dirt a mirror and the membrane an embryo (3.38–39); its seat is the senses, mind and understanding, through which it deludes the embodied one (3.40); controlling the senses first, and knowing what is beyond the understanding and steadying the self by the self, one is to slay it (3.41–43).

relations.note: desire covers knowledge and deludes the embodied one

notes: The skeleton records the same passage as the obstacle obs:kama-the-enemy.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, each family has eternal family dharmas, which perish when the family is destroyed; then adharma prevails, the family's women are corrupted, varṇa-mixture arises, the ancestors fall, and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell (1.40–44).

relations.note: their loss leads to varṇa-mixture (Arjuna's argument)

name: The last thought and resolve at death

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Abiding in the brāhmī sthiti even at the time of death (antakāle 'pi), one attains brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).

notes: The Gītā develops the theme of the last moment at 8.5–13 (outside this chunk). Bhagavad Gītā 1–3 contributes only 2.72 (antakāle 'pi); the Gītā's main passage is 8.5–6 (skeleton cpt:last-thought-at-death).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Chapters 1–3 name the goal in several ways without systematising them: fitness for immortality (amṛtatva, 2.15); freedom from the bondage of birth and going to the state free from ill (padam anāmayam, 2.51); brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72); attaining the highest (param, 3.19); perfection (saṃsiddhi, 3.20); release from actions (3.31).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should act with a view to holding the world together (3.20): people do what the best person does and follow the standard he sets (3.21); Kṛṣṇa himself acts for this reason (3.22–24); the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant attached to action (3.25–26, 3.29).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: A person does not attain actionlessness by not undertaking actions, nor perfection by renunciation alone (3.4).

relations.note: no one can in fact stay without action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument: varṇa-mixture leads family-destroyers and the family to hell (1.42); those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell there for an indefinite time, as tradition says (1.44).

name: Action without attachment to its fruit

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action performed with a right only to the act and not to its fruit, without attachment, the same in success and failure, 'established in yoga' (2.47–48); yoked with understanding it leaves behind good and evil deeds and frees from the bondage of birth (2.50–51); undertaken with the organs of action by one whose senses are controlled by the mind (3.7); done for sacrifice (3.9), for the holding together of the world (3.20, 3.25), and finally resigned to Kṛṣṇa (3.30).

relations.note: the wise yoked with understanding, abandoning the fruit, go to the state free from ill; the unattached reach the highest
The practice of the karmayoga commitment.

name: The self is not the agent; the guṇas act

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self neither slays nor is slain, and the one who knows it cannot be said to slay or cause to slay (2.19–21); actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti, and only one deluded by the sense of 'I' thinks 'I am the doer', while the knower of the truth sees that the guṇas move among the guṇas and is not attached (3.27–28).

relations.note: what the self does not do is done by the guṇas

name: The real (sat) and the unreal (asat)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The unreal has no coming to be and the real no ceasing to be; the seers of reality have seen the final truth of both (2.16).

notes: The commentators divide on what sat and asat denote in 2.16 and on whether the verse speaks of existence or of reality; it is later cited in debates on causation. Not the same as data/'s cpt:sat-and-asat (being and non-being at the origin).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The embodied one obtains another body as it passes through childhood, youth and old age (2.13); it casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones as a man changes clothes (2.22); death is certain for the born and birth for the dead (2.27); freedom from the bondage of birth is gained by abandoning the fruit of action (2.51).

name: Equanimity (samatva)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Being the same in pain and pleasure makes one fit for immortality (2.15); pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat are to be made the same (2.38); equanimity is called yoga (2.48); the one of steady wisdom is unagitated in sorrow, without longing in pleasure, and neither rejoices nor hates (2.56–57); the sense-contacts are to be endured (2.14).

notes: Merger: probably the same as the skeleton's cpt:equanimity ('Evenness of mind (samatva)', BhG 2.48); both extractors used this id, so it is kept; flagged for the de-duplication pass.

name: The hierarchy of senses, mind, understanding and what is beyond them

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The senses are high; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the understanding; what is higher than the understanding is 'he' (3.42); knowing this, steadying the self by the self, one slays desire (3.43). Parallel series in Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11.

notes: Parallels Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11, which has a longer series.

name: The person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Asked for the marks of one of steady wisdom established in samādhi (2.54), Kṛṣṇa describes one who gives up all desires and is content in the self by the self (2.55); is unshaken by sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger (2.56); unattached, neither rejoicing nor hating (2.57); withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.58), the taste itself ceasing on seeing the highest (2.59); sits yoked, intent on Kṛṣṇa, senses mastered (2.61, 2.68); moves among objects with mastered senses and attains serenity (2.64–65); is awake where beings sleep (2.69); is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved (2.70); without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.71). This is the brahmic state, reached which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72).

members: gives up all desires; content in the self by the self (2.55)
unshaken in sorrow, without craving in pleasure; free from passion, fear, anger (2.56)
withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.58)
even the taste ceases on seeing the highest (2.59)
awake in the night of beings (2.69)

relations.note: abiding in this state even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna's own dharma as a kṣatriya is to fight a battle in accordance with dharma, the best thing for a kṣatriya and an open door to heaven; abandoning it incurs sin and disgrace (2.31–37). One's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's well performed; death in it is better; another's brings fear (3.35).

relations.note: Kṛṣṇa's argument from svadharma answers Arjuna's argument from family dharma.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Heaven as the reward of the warrior slain in a dharmic battle (2.32, 2.37), and as the aim of the ritual-minded criticised in 2.43.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make every being act (3.5); actions are done by them (3.27); the knower sees 'guṇas move among guṇas' (3.28); those deluded by them are attached to their actions (3.29); desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, and Arjuna is to be free of them (2.45). Chapters 1–3 name sattva (2.45) and rajas (3.37) only.

name: The twofold commitment (dvividhā niṣṭhā): jñāna-yoga and karma-yoga

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Kṛṣṇa taught of old a twofold commitment (niṣṭhā): by jñānayoga for the Sāṃkhyas and by karmayoga for the Yogins (3.3); freedom from action is not reached by not acting, nor perfection by renunciation alone (3.4). Cf. the understanding 'according to sāṃkhya' and 'according to yoga' (2.39).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, when adharma prevails the family's women are corrupted and varṇa-mixture arises, bringing hell to the family-destroyers and the family and the fall of the ancestors, and uprooting the dharmas of birth-group and family (1.41–43). Kṛṣṇa uses 'saṅkara' of the confusion he would cause if he stopped acting (3.24).

name: The wheel of sacrifice (yajña-cakra)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Prajāpati created beings together with sacrifice, bidding them multiply by it; gods and humans nourish one another through it and so attain the highest good; one who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eaters of the sacrificial remainder are freed from faults (3.10–13); beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice, sacrifice from action, action from brahman, brahman from the imperishable (3.14–15); one who does not keep this wheel turning lives in vain (3.16). Action other than for sacrifice binds (3.9).

notes: The commentators divide on brahman and akṣara in 3.15 (most: the Veda and the imperishable supreme).
